title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
In this analysis, I look at women whose income was below the poverty level in the past 12 months across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Data collected on vulnerable populations can be used both to understand and provide necessary resources to those populations, so the reliability of the data is important for ensuring that those populations are accurately represented.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe/estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        250    85    34  
 2 Wyoming County, New York        2364   439    18.6
 3 Yates County, New York          1780   300    16.9
 4 Washington County, New York     3436   566    16.5
 5 Greene County, New York         2803   461    16.4

 9 Fulton County, New York         3764   555    14.7

Hamilton County has the largest relative margin of error, at 34%.

text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     8
2 Low confidence     35
3 Moderate           19


Eight counties out of the total 62 fall into the category of “High Confidence” when it is defined at a threshold margin of error of 5%. Nineteen counties fall into the category of “Moderate Confidence” when it is defined at a threshold of 10%. Thirty-five counties were classified as “Low Confidence.”

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       20723   1434  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York      3616    350   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       211879   5751 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       19066   1290  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York   6786    535   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York        5499    528   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          8       1465609.
2 Low confidence          35         66228.
3 Moderate                19        306814.


In order to compare the average population of counties in each reliability category, I have to group each observation by their reliability category and then take the average of each grouping’s population estimate.
Using the same thresholds as before, the average population of high-confidence counties is 1,465,609, while the average population of low-confidence counties is 66,228. This suggests that larger counties are counted more accurately than smaller counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The top 5 counties with the largest margins of error were Hamilton County, Wyoming County, Yates County, Washington County, and Greene County. Of these 5 counties, Washington had the largest population, totaling to almost 61,000 residents, while Hamilton County had the smallest population, totaling to about 5100. All 5 counties had margins of error above 16%, with Hamilton County having the largest margin of error at 34%. This suggests there is more accurate data collected about low-income women in larger counties (like those comprising New York City) than the smaller counties upstate. However, this is not surprising from a statistical standpoint. Unlike the Decennial Census, which aims to count everyone, the ACS makes estimates for a given geography based on sample data. Therefore, when the samples are smaller, each unit increase in the margin of error accounts for a much larger percentage than for a larger sample.
If a state agency were to allocate funding for economic development opportunities for women based on the percentage of low-income women as compiled by the ACS without accounting for margins of error, the agency might misjudge the extent of poverty as an issue for female residents in smaller counties versus larger counties. The 2023 ACS estimates that about 5% of Hamilton’s population were women whose income was below the poverty level in the past 12 months. However, the margin of error suggests that as much as 6.5% of Hamilton’s population may have been low-income women. Without taking into account the margin of error, however, the state agency might decide that Hamilton County doesn’t meet the minimum threshold required to be eligible for the funding.

title: Week 3: GGPLOT & Addressing Margins of Error
text:
Key Concepts
Visualizing data is important because different datasets can have similar (or even identical) summary statistics but look very different (i.e. Ansombe’s Quartet).

A plot is a mapping from columns in a dataset to visual properties on a page. Known as “Grammer of Graphics” (“GG”).
Ex: estimate column -> position on y-axis, population column -> postition on x-axis

GGPLOT Basics plot1 <- ggplot(data) + this creates a blank canvas with your data as reference aes() + despite the name, “aesthetics” refers to column assignment geom_something() shape/type of chart
“Decorations” (i.e. colors, etc.) go in geom_*() portion of code, not aes()
Options for geom:

histogram
point (for scatterplot)
boxplot
col (for barchart)
line
errorbar

Combining 2 geom:

Each type has its own aes specfications
Ex: geom_col() has aes( x = somevalue, y = somevalue), while geom_errorbar() has aes(ymin = somevalue, ymax = somevalue)

Extra:

facet_wrap() for creating multiple charts side-by-side for comparison
coord_flip() to flip x and y axis orientation
mutate(str_remove(column, “__“)) to remove some text/edit a column
Can use theme_minimal() for graphs as a shortcut for nice aesthetics
labs() for the labels of a graph

Census Bureau uses coefficient of variation (“CV”).

CV is a relative measure of sampling error, tied to the 90% confidence interval.
Census assumes a low CV of 15% (high reliability), medium of 15-30%, and high > 30% (low reliability, high sampling error)

Derived uncertainty

Cannot simply add up or multiply margins of error when comparing different estimates
In tidycensus: moe_sum() will properly add moe’s for different estimates

Also: moe_prop() for one estimate as a share of another, and moe_ratio() for ratio of 2 variables


Change over time with ACS data

5-year ACS estimates have overlapping time periods when comparing years that are close together (ex: 2023 and 2022)
Instead, use ACS years that do not have overlapping periods (ex: 2018 and 2023)
Standard error of difference and confidence interval of change to determine if the difference in estimates between years is real (i.e. does not include zero)

title: Week 4: Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
Key Concepts
Overview of Geography & Coordinate Reference Systems

Geographic: latitude and longitude, measured in degrees

Geographers draw different ellipsoids to fit different areas of the Earth better
Ex: North American Datum 1927 (NAD27) based on Clarke’s ellipsoid from 1866
NAD83 based on satellite imagery; more accurate than NAD27 and most commonly used in U.S. today
WGS84 is the standard for GPS because it’s global

Projected: flattens 3D to 2D, measured in ft and meters

Projections distort shape, area, distance, and/or direction
Every projection has a “line of tangency” where there is no distortion
Cylindrical: northern and southern extremities of Earth most distorted - ex: Mercator
Conic: best for northern hemisphere (ex: Canada, U.S., Russia, China)
Planar: best for singular landmass (ex: Australia)

Projection for Philadelphia: PA southern state plane (2272)

Spatial features (Sf) and relevant commands in R:

st_crs(your data) to view crs of your data
st_set_crs() to add correct label (if missing)

if missing, may need to guess and check to find right crs

st_transform() to change the projection of your data
st_buffer() to create buffer around object

units will match that of the object/layer

st_intersects() is /not/ the same as st_touches()
st_filter() to select geographies that are completely within set buffer distance
st_union() to unify everything selected
st_intersection() to get common area
st_join() behaves like a left join for spatial datasets
st_distance() to returns a matrix of distances between all objects within 2 datasets
st_disjoint if geometries have no point in common (i.e. are completely separate)

title: Week 7: Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Key Concepts
Summary of linear regression transformations:

Log of a variable: Corrects for right skew; “a 1% increase in x → β/100 increase in y”

If both the predictor and the outcome are logged, the interpretation becomes “a 1% increase in x goes with about β % change in y (an elasticity)”
If the outcome is logged but the predictor is not, the interpretation becomes “a 1-unit increase in x goes with about 100·β % change in y”

Square of a variable: To correct for a curve or plateau; included in model as x + x^2

Interpretation: positive linear term, negative squared term → rises, then levels off or falls

Categorical variable: Should use if it makes sense logically (ex: housing type), or if a numeric variable seems to have specific breaks

Coefficients are written for k-1 categories and compared to the “reference” level

Ex: If Downtown is the reference level, then the coefficient of Northeast_district is relative to the Downtown area

case_when(): writing the rules out
cut(): determining the breakpoints
Extra small groups should be merged before cross-validation, or else it will mess up the predictive power of the model

Interaction variable: Reflects how a variable interacts differently based on the categorical variable

Ex: Income has a different impact on median rent based on the neighborhood
Written as: variable * categorical variable

Fixed effect: Variable that captures some general categorical effect, usually location (ex: neighborhood, district, etc.)

Clustering & Moran’s I:

Tobler’s First Law of Geography: All things are related, but near things are more related
Moran’s I: the slope of the relationship between average of k neighbors’ residuals vs observation’s residuals

Equation: Wij * Sum of (individual error - avg error)(neighbor’s error - avg error) / sum of (individual error - avg error)^2

Top part of equation functions like a matrix multiplied by a weight
Weight = number of observations / number of neighbor pairs

Ex: (Error A - avg error)(Error B - avg error) + (Error B - avg error)(Error C - avg error) + … (*2, to account for reciprocal nature of neighbors) / (Error A - avg error)^2 + (Error B - avg error)^2 + …
Moran’s I can fall between 0 and 1; a higher value means more clustering (zero signifies randomness)

Monte Carlo simulation: shuffles residuals multiple times to calculate Moran’s I; if the “real” I is larger than the simulation I, then the clustering is significant
Clustering can signify that our model is missing a spatial variable
Spatial lag is good for inference about spillovers, but not appropriate for predictive models

Part 1b: Join by what
How much has income changed since 2015? Pull the older estimates. No geometry is needed, because this is just a table.

income_15 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(med_inc_15 = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2015,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = FALSE
) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_inc_15E, med_inc_15M)

nrow(income_15)

[1] 384

nrow(philly_tracts)

[1] 391


Stop and look: The row counts are different. Before you join, predict why.
Row counts are different because the number of census tracts have changed in the past ~10 years.
Now join the 2015 table onto your tracts. The key is the column both tables share.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(income_15, by = "GEOID")

nrow(philly_tracts)   # did the row count change?

[1] 391


The row count for philly_tracts did not change.
The rule: after every join, count rows and count NAs.

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    no_2015_match = sum(is.na(med_inc_15E))

Key Concepts
Linear regression can be used for inference (traditional statistics) or prediction (machine learning)

Example: Rent as a function of income

For inference, interested in slope/coefficient as statistically significant
But for predictions, the statistical significance of any one coefficient is less important
Want to know where rents exceed our expectations, given a specific median income
More interested in knowing how well model predicts values on unseen data - we may justify including an insignificant variable if it increases our predictive power


Scale of machine learning models:
Simpler - Linear - Lasso/Ridge - Logistic - Trees & Random Forest - Boosting - Neural Networks - More complex

Parametric: assumes a functional form
Non-parametric: more difficult to interpret

Noisy: i.e. uncertain; data is reflected in model’s residuals (larger) and slope (flatter)
For predictions, we use test and training datasets for create our models

Typical split: 80% training, 20% test
Want to minimize RMSE

Ex: our rent model is off by $300 on average

K-fold cross validation: breaking up data into “k” number of folds (5, 10, etc.)

Training dataset = k-1 folds; run “k” number of times to find an average RMSE

Overfitting: model has been tuned to the nopise in our ttraining dataset; this model fails to work with test/new data
Multi-collinearity: variables are highly correlated

Less of a problem for prediction than inference

Part 3 — Adjudicating
Sorting the article’s claims into three buckets produces the following results:
Supported: There was a significant increase in the immigrant population in the neighborhood of Mayfair between 2017 and 2022. Taking into account the margins of error for each estimate in this analysis reveals that the difference between the two years is unlikely to be zero, given the z-score and the range of the confidence interval of the difference.
Not supported: Mayfair’s population did not significantly increase between 2017 and 2022. Analyzing the difference in the population estimates between the two years did not produce significant z-scores for any of the tracts, signaling that the changes in population estimates are unlikely to be non-zero.
Cannot be determined: It is unclear whether Philadelphia’s population significantly increased between 2023 and 2024. The Census Bureau does not list margins of error for those county-wide population estimates in the 5-year ACS data, therefore I cannot conduct the same analysis for this claim as I did for Mayfair. This also means that I can’t verify how Mayfair’s demographic changes compare to Philadelphia’s.

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.407  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    h_count = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1)),
    h_density = h_count / area_sqmi,
    road_count = lengths(st_intersects(., layer2)))

f2 <- perc_no_veh ~ perc_poverty + perc_high_edu + perc_under18 + h_count

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "h_count",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Properties coded as single, multi, or apt")

f3 <- perc_no_veh ~ perc_poverty + perc_high_edu + perc_under18 + h_density

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "h_density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "Density with respect to tract area")

f4 <- perc_no_veh ~ perc_poverty + perc_high_edu + perc_under18 + road_count

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "road_count",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "Roads coded as arterials or car-oriented")

Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Your answer: Housing density (defined as number of housing units divided by tract area) marginally lowered the RMSE (with respect to the original model). Housing count and car-centric road count did not significantly impact the RMSE. I expected that housing density would be more useful than housing count, given that housing density more accurately reflects the physical conditions of walkable neighborhoods and also controls for tract size. I suspect that car-centric roads as a variable had less of an impact on the model due to the fact that these types of roads tend to be larger roads that span multiple tracts and may even cut across the whole city, therefore it is hard to judge the impact of any of these roads on any one census tract.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(perc_no_veh ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = perc_no_veh ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-18.739  -3.562  -0.828   3.135  34.716 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     24.54124    0.93761  26.174  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi      -3.35728    0.34012  -9.871  < 2e-16 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2)  0.13716    0.02558   5.363 1.41e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 6.818 on 388 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4151,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4121 
F-statistic: 137.7 on 2 and 388 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = perc_no_veh)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  81
2 Inner 137
3 Outer 173


Code
m_cat <- lm(perc_no_veh ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = perc_no_veh ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-20.505  -4.692  -1.116   3.463  37.652 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  20.5054     0.8120  25.253  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner    -6.0589     1.0243  -5.915 7.29e-09 ***
ringOuter   -13.0551     0.9839 -13.269  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.308 on 388 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3281,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3246 
F-statistic: 94.71 on 2 and 388 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Part 7: Reflection

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.

Your answer:

Housing density lowered the CV RMSE the most: from 7.31 in the baseline model to 6.97. I was disappointed that the log of housing density worsened the RMSE rather than improving it; I really thought the log would help with the skew.
All else equal, a one percent increase in the share of residents under the age of 18 in a tract decreases the share of households without cars by 0.45%.
Although the model was supposed to help predict ridership for new public transportation investments, I probably should have included proximity to existing public transportation stops as a variable. Center City has the largest residuals with the final model, and even though I tried to account for walkability by measuring housing density, I think the concentration of public transportation options in the area may be a more influential factor in determining a household’s car ownership than simply walkability. I would be able to get public transit stop data (buses, L line, B line, etc.) from Open Data Philly.
